#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""J4 attack (i): classify every keyword hit (sweep_hits.json) and every
comparison-shaped line the keyword regex misses, as conditional_statement,
design_figure or outcome. 'outcome' = states or implies, as an outcome,
prediction, success criterion or verdict, that a deployed/standardized row sits
below its matched rho or that a curve is broken, weakened or safe (TH-1).
Manual classes are the red team's reading of each sentence in context."""
import json
import re
import yaml

hits = json.load(open("sweep_hits.json"))
CS, DF, OUTC = "conditional_statement", "design_figure", "outcome"
NEG = "negation or outcome-discipline sentence; asserts that no verdict is made"
manual = {
    0: (CS, NEG), 1: (CS, NEG), 2: (CS, "exclusion of the proposal's (C3) verdict and figures"),
    3: (CS, "(C3') conditional on H-DL-1, H-DL-2 and MM-1; states no sign"),
    4: (CS, NEG), 5: (CS, "cell-verdict naming rule; conditional on OB-1; not a curve verdict"),
    6: (CS, "cell verdict conditional on OB-1; not a curve verdict"), 7: (CS, "DC-H5 marking (OB-4)"),
    8: (CS, "cost row conditional on H-DL-1/H-DL-2, no direction against matched rho"),
    9: (CS, "quantifier statement of the procedure"), 10: (CS, "method ceiling; every item conditional"),
    11: (CS, NEG), 12: (CS, "falsification threshold on log2 kappa; keyword 'below' not about rho"),
    13: (CS, "cost-input provenance statement"), 14: (CS, "convention statement (CORR-20260922-81aeab)"),
    15: (CS, "role of a cost input"), 16: (CS, "metric label; its minimum_effect is NO PREDICTION"),
    17: (CS, NEG), 18: (CS, "falsification rule; conditional; contradicts nothing"),
    19: (CS, NEG), 20: (CS, NEG), 21: (CS, "exclusion of the proposal's (C3) verdict and figures"),
    22: (CS, "arm label (cell-verdict trichotomy)"), 23: (CS, "procedure"), 24: (CS, "cell verdict conditional on OB-1"),
    25: (CS, NEG), 26: (CS, "sampling procedure; keyword 'below' incidental"),
    27: (CS, "pointer; keyword 'below' incidental"), 28: (CS, NEG), 29: (CS, NEG),
    30: (CS, "control definition (PTM-D rows); its printed values are design figures"),
    31: (CS, "metric label"), 32: (CS, "seed rule; keyword 'below' incidental"), 33: (CS, "function name"),
    34: (DF, "toy-cell degeneracy verdicts (admissibility arithmetic); no deployed row"),
    35: (CS, "evidence-mapping rule; 'weakens' refers to hypothesis parts, not curves"),
    36: (CS, "cost-model disclosure"), 37: (CS, "cost-model disclosure (overestimate on the rho arm)"),
    38: (CS, "machine-model statement"), 39: (CS, "tradeoff statement"), 40: (CS, "tradeoff statement"),
    41: (CS, NEG), 42: (CS, "artifact label (conditional)"), 43: (CS, NEG), 44: (CS, NEG),
    45: (CS, NEG), 46: (CS, NEG),
    47: (DF, "matched rho values; 'below' compares two rho conventions, not a row against rho"),
    48: (CS, "quantifier statement"), 49: (CS, "method ceiling"),
    50: (DF, "PTM-D synthetic rows at P_REF only; not a deployed-row statement (see PTM-D finding)"),
    51: (CS, "pointer"), 52: (CS, "pointer"), 53: (CS, "DC-H5 discharge statement"), 54: (CS, "pointer"),
    55: (CS, "read-attestation path; keyword incidental"), 56: (CS, "authority statement; keyword incidental"),
    57: (CS, NEG), 67: (CS, NEG), 80: (CS, "sampler description; keyword incidental"),
    92: (CS, "extraction note; keyword incidental"), 93: (CS, "code-block role"),
    94: (DF, "format string of the matched-rho design figure"), 95: (DF, "format string (record_minus_matched diagnostic)"),
    96: (DF, "JSON key"), 97: (DF, "format string (prime-control matched rho)"), 98: (DF, "JSON key"),
    99: (CS, "code docstring; " + NEG), 100: (CS, "printed header; " + NEG), 101: (CS, "printed header; " + NEG),
    102: (DF, "format string of the rho row"), 103: (DF, "format string of the PTM-D rows"),
    104: (CS, "code-block role"), 105: (DF, "calibration output label"), 106: (DF, "dry-call output label"),

    109: (DF, "toy admissibility output label"),
}
out = []
for i, h in enumerate(hits):
    if i in manual:
        cls, why = manual[i]
    elif h["kind"] == "embedded_output":
        cls, why = DF, "embedded output of committed design code (C-2/C-3/C-4/C-5/C-6/C-7), labelled design figure"
    else:

                      "class": DF, "reason": "printed sensitivity grid of d_fc (design figure)", "text": s[:160] + " ..."})
H = yaml.safe_load(open("/home/user/crypto-autoresearcher/ledger/hypotheses/H-BINSTD-0dd2ce.yaml").read())["hypothesis"]
extra.append({"file": "H", "where": "hypothesis.asymptotic_note", "class": CS,
              "reason": "family-level exponent statement conditional on H-DL-2; 'No row-level statement follows from it'; "
                        "the phrase 'the known composite-degree GHS phenomenon' carries no citation or provenance",
              "text": " ".join(H["asymptotic_note"].split())})
res = {"keyword_hits": out, "comparison_shaped_extra": extra,
       "counts": {"keyword_hits": len(out), "extra": len(extra),
                  "by_class": {c: sum(1 for x in out + extra if x["class"] == c) for c in (CS, DF, OUTC)},
                  "c4_lines_with_negative_delta_work": sum(1 for x in extra if x.get("negative_delta_work"))},
       "TH-1_fired": any(x["class"] == OUTC for x in out + extra)}
json.dump(res, open("rt_classify_out.json", "w"), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)
print(json.dumps(res["counts"]), "TH-1_fired:", res["TH-1_fired"])
print([x["text"][:60] + " ..." + x["text"][-50:] for x in extra if x.get("negative_delta_work")])

scripts.role: Independent MM-1 implementation written from the specification's cost_model text; C-4 parser.
scripts.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Red-team independent implementation of machine model MM-1, written from the
TEXT of experiments/EXP-BINSTD-f442a9/specification.yaml cost_model (not from
the committed cost_table block). Where the text is silent, the choice made here
is named in TEXT_SILENT and reported. Review computation only: arithmetic on the
contract's model and on published group orders. No group, curve or cover.
Importing executes nothing."""
import json
import math
import re
import sys

# Spec constants, read from the cost_model text.
P_REF = 2.0 ** 20            # "reference P_REF = 2^20"
RHO_AREA = 2.0 ** 16         # "RHO_AREA = 2^16 bits per processor-equivalent"
RHO_MULTS = 10               # "per-iteration cost 10 N^2 bit operations"
DP_PER_PROC = 2.0 ** 10      # "distinguished points numbering P x 2^10"
DP_BITS = 3                  # "3 log2 l bits each"
P_LA_MAX = 2.0 ** 10         # "parallel over at most P_LA_MAX = 2^10 nodes"
TEXT_SILENT = {
    "descent_trial_cost": "spec gives 'g! q trials' without a per-trial cost; taken equal to the relation trial cost g^2(1+log2 q) F_q mults",
    "phase_memory": "spec says FC = (P + memory_bits/RHO_AREA) x wall per phase, summed, without naming which memory each phase holds; taken: relation memory during relation collection and descent and map, LA memory during LA",
    "map_parallelism": "spec silent; taken as 1 processor",
    "mem_column": "spec silent; taken as max(relation memory, LA memory)",
}


def L(x):
    return math.log2(x)


def lsum(*xs):
    """log2 of a sum of 2^x terms (ignores -inf)."""
    xs = [x for x in xs if x != float("-inf")]
    top = max(xs)
    return top + L(sum(2.0 ** (x - top) for x in xs))


def rho(log2_l, k, N, P=P_REF, area=RHO_AREA, dp_per_proc=DP_PER_PROC, dp_bits=DP_BITS):
    W = 0.5 * (L(math.pi) + log2_l - L(4 * k))           # sqrt(pi l / (4k))
    t = L(RHO_MULTS * N * N)                               # 10 N^2 bit ops / iteration
    ndp = L(P) + L(dp_per_proc)                            # P x 2^10 DPs
    mem = ndp + L(dp_bits * log2_l)                        # bits
    # theta set so the table holds P x 2^10 points: theta = ndp / W, 1/theta = W / ndp
    wall = lsum(W - L(P), W - ndp) + t                     # (W/P + 1/theta) t
    fc = lsum(L(P), mem - L(area)) + wall                  # (P + mem/area) x wall
    return dict(W=W, t=t, work=W + t, mem=mem, wall=wall, fc=fc)


def ic(c, n, g, log2_l, N, log2_kappa, P=P_REF, area=RHO_AREA, p_la_max=P_LA_MAX):
    lq = float(c)                                          # log2 q
    fq = 2 * L(c)                                          # F_q mult = c^2 bit ops
    trial = L(g * g * (1 + c)) + fq                        # g^2 (1 + log2 q) F_q mults
    rel = log2_kappa + (2 - 2 / g) * lq + trial            # kappa q^(2-2/g) trials
    D = (1 - 1 / g) * lq                                   # log2 of factor base size
    w = 2 * g                                              # row weight
    la = 2 * D + L(3 * w * log2_l + 7 * log2_l ** 2)       # D^2 (3 w log2 l + 7 (log2 l)^2)
    mem_la = D + L(w * (D + 1) + 4 * log2_l)               # D (w (log2 D + 1) + 4 log2 l)
    mem_rel = L(4) + D + L((g + 2) * (lq + 1))             # 4 D (g + 2)(log2 q + 1)
    desc = L(math.factorial(g)) + lq + trial               # g! q trials (TEXT_SILENT)
    mp = L(2 * n * g * g) + 2 * L(N)                       # 2 n g^2 F_(2^N) mults
    pla = min(P, p_la_max)
    wall = lsum(rel - L(P), la - L(pla), desc - L(P), mp)
    fc = lsum(lsum(L(P), mem_rel - L(area)) + rel - L(P),
              lsum(L(pla), mem_la - L(area)) + la - L(pla),
              lsum(L(P), mem_rel - L(area)) + desc - L(P),
              lsum(0.0, mem_rel - L(area)) + mp)
    return dict(rel=rel, la=la, desc=desc, map=mp, work=lsum(rel, la, desc, mp), D=D, w=w,
                mem_rel=mem_rel, mem_la=mem_la, mem=max(mem_rel, mem_la), wall=wall, fc=fc)


def parse_c4(text):
    rows, lanes, ptmd = {}, [], {}
    cur = None
    for line in text.splitlines():
        s = line.strip()
        m = re.match(r"ROW (\S+) N=(\d+) k=(\d+) log2_l=([\d.]+) matched_rho_iters_log2=([\d.]+) rho_work=([\d.]+)"
                     r" rho_mem=([\d.]+) rho_wall=([\d.]+) rho_fc=([\d.]+)", s)
        if m:
            cur = m.group(1)
            rows[cur] = dict(N=int(m.group(2)), k=int(m.group(3)), log2_l=float(m.group(4)),
                             W=float(m.group(5)), work=float(m.group(6)), mem=float(m.group(7)),
                             wall=float(m.group(8)), fc=float(m.group(9)))
            continue
        m = re.match(r"LANE (\S+) c=(\d+) n=(\d+) m=(\d+) g=(\d+) regime_ratio=([\d.]+) (\S+) log2kappa=([\d.]+) \|"
                     r" rel=([\d.]+) la=([\d.]+) desc=([\d.]+) map=([\d.]+) work=([\d.]+) \| la_dim=([\d.]+)"
                     r" la_weight=(\d+) mem_rel=([\d.]+) mem_la=([\d.]+) mem=([\d.]+) \| wall=([\d.]+) fc=([\d.]+) \|"
                     r" cond_delta_work=([-\d.]+) cond_delta_mem=([-\d.]+) cond_delta_fc=([-\d.]+)", s)
        if m:
            keys = ["role", "c", "n", "m", "g", "ratio", "label", "log2kappa", "rel", "la", "desc", "map", "work",
                    "la_dim", "la_weight", "mem_rel", "mem_la", "mem", "wall", "fc", "d_work", "d_mem", "d_fc"]
            vals = list(m.groups())
            d = dict(zip(keys, vals))
            for kk in keys:
                if kk not in ("role", "label"):
                    d[kk] = float(d[kk])
            d["row"] = cur
            lanes.append(d)
            continue
        m = re.match(r"(\S+) \(a\) rho-as-IC: d_work=([-\d.]+) d_mem=([-\d.]+) d_fc=([-\d.]+) \| \(b\) rho time \+ 2\^40"
                     r" entries: d_work=([-\d.]+) d_mem=([-\d.]+) d_fc=([-\d.]+)", s)
        if m:
            ptmd[m.group(1)] = [float(x) for x in m.groups()[1:]]
    return rows, lanes, ptmd


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("rt_mm1 is a library; see rt_recompute.py")

scripts.role: J4 attack (ii): row-by-row recomputation of C-4 with rt_mm1.py and field-by-field diff.
scripts.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""J4 (ii): recompute the C-4 cost table row by row with the red team's own MM-1
implementation (rt_mm1.py, written from the spec text) and compare every printed
field. Inputs: the audit sheet's embedded C-4 output (the contract's frozen
design figure) and the published group orders (rt_orders.json, from openssl)."""
import json
import math
import re
import yaml

import rt_mm1 as M

A = ("/home/user/crypto-autoresearcher/coordination/goals/GOAL-ECDLP2M-001/batches/BATCH-2e63c3/"
     "design/TASK-20261002-9f9ce5/proof-search-map-audit.yaml")
sc = yaml.safe_load(open(A, encoding="utf-8").read())["audit_sheet"]["session_computations"]
c4 = sc["C-4"]["output_run2"]
orders = json.load(open("rt_orders.json"))
rows, lanes, ptmd = M.parse_c4(c4)

KN = {"c2pnb176v1": (176, 11), "c2pnb208w1": (208, 13), "c2pnb272w1": (272, 17),
      "c2pnb304w1": (304, 19), "c2pnb368w1": (368, 23)}
report = {"rho": {}, "lanes": [], "max_abs_diff": {}, "charged_terms_every_row": None,
          "no_cost_row_lanes": [], "text_silent_choices": M.TEXT_SILENT}

# rho per row
for name, r in rows.items():
    N, k = KN[name]
    lg = orders[name]["log2_l"]
    mine = M.rho(lg, k, N)
    report["rho"][name] = {
        "log2_l_published": round(lg, 6), "log2_l_c4": r["log2_l"],
        "W_mine": round(mine["W"], 3), "W_c4": r["W"],
        "work": [round(mine["work"], 2), r["work"]], "mem": [round(mine["mem"], 2), r["mem"]],
        "wall": [round(mine["wall"], 2), r["wall"]], "fc": [round(mine["fc"], 2), r["fc"]],
    }
    for key in ("work", "mem", "wall", "fc"):
        report["max_abs_diff"]["rho_" + key] = max(report["max_abs_diff"].get("rho_" + key, 0.0),
                                                   abs(round(mine[key], 2) - r[key]))

# IC lanes
fields = ["rel", "la", "desc", "map", "work", "mem_rel", "mem_la", "mem", "wall", "fc"]
all_charged = True
for d in lanes:
    name = d["row"]
    N, k = KN[name]
    lg = orders[name]["log2_l"]
    g = int(d["g"])
    assert g == 2 ** (int(d["m"]) - 1), "genus is not 2^(m-1)"
    mine = M.ic(int(d["c"]), int(d["n"]), g, lg, N, d["log2kappa"])
    rr = M.rho(lg, k, N)
    deltas = {"d_work": mine["work"] - rr["work"], "d_mem": mine["mem"] - rr["mem"], "d_fc": mine["fc"] - rr["fc"]}
    entry = {"row": name, "role": d["role"], "c": int(d["c"]), "g": g, "kappa_label": d["label"],
             "log2kappa": d["log2kappa"]}
    for f in fields:
        entry[f] = [round(mine[f], 2), d[f]]
        report["max_abs_diff"][f] = max(report["max_abs_diff"].get(f, 0.0), abs(round(mine[f], 2) - d[f]))
    for f in ("d_work", "d_mem", "d_fc"):
        entry[f] = [round(deltas[f], 2), d[f]]
        report["max_abs_diff"][f] = max(report["max_abs_diff"].get(f, 0.0), abs(round(deltas[f], 2) - d[f]))
    entry["la_dim"] = [round(mine["D"], 2), d["la_dim"]]
    entry["la_weight"] = [mine["w"], d["la_weight"]]
    charged = all(math.isfinite(mine[t]) for t in ("rel", "la", "desc", "map", "mem_rel", "mem_la")) \
        and all(math.isfinite(d[t]) for t in ("rel", "la", "desc", "map", "mem_rel", "mem_la"))
    entry["la_desc_mem_charged"] = charged
    all_charged = all_charged and charged
    report["lanes"].append(entry)
report["charged_terms_every_row"] = all_charged
report["cost_lines"] = len(lanes)
report["cost_cells"] = sorted({(d["row"], d["role"]) for d in lanes})

# Lanes printed as NO COST ROW: check the regime ratio g / log2 q from printed c, g.
for line in c4.splitlines():
    m = re.search(r"LANE (\S+) c=(\d+) n=(\d+) m=(\d+) g=(\d+) regime_ratio g/log2q=([\d.]+) > 1.0", line)
    if m:
        c, g = int(m.group(2)), int(m.group(5))
        report["no_cost_row_lanes"].append({"role": m.group(1), "c": c, "m": int(m.group(4)), "g": g,
                                            "ratio_mine": round(g / c, 3), "ratio_printed": float(m.group(6)),
                                            "g_is_2^(m-1)": g == 2 ** (int(m.group(4)) - 1)})
json.dump(report, open("rt_recompute_out.json", "w"), indent=1)
print("cost lines", len(lanes), "cells", len(report["cost_cells"]))
print("max_abs_diff", json.dumps({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in report["max_abs_diff"].items()}))
print("LA, descent and memory charged in every cost line:", all_charged)
print("no-cost-row lanes", len(report["no_cost_row_lanes"]),
      "all ratio>1 recomputed:", all(x["ratio_mine"] > 1 for x in report["no_cost_row_lanes"]))
for name, r in report["rho"].items():
    print("RHO", name, r)

the contract's frozen C-3 printed output and the published orders, then run the
committed cost_table block on it and diff against the frozen C-4 text. This is
synthetic input through committed code (review computation); it is not ARM-S0 and
not ARM-COST, and it computes nothing on any group, curve or cover."""
import importlib.util
import io
import json
import re
import sys
import contextlib
import yaml

A = ("/home/user/crypto-autoresearcher/coordination/goals/GOAL-ECDLP2M-001/batches/BATCH-2e63c3/"
     "design/TASK-20261002-9f9ce5/proof-search-map-audit.yaml")
BLOCKS = "blocks/"


def load_block(name):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, BLOCKS + name + ".py")
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
    return mod


def build():
    sc = yaml.safe_load(open(A, encoding="utf-8").read())["audit_sheet"]["session_computations"]
    c3 = sc["C-3"]["output_run2"]
    orders = json.load(open("rt_orders.json"))
    census = {"rows": {}, "prime_controls": {}, "fixtures": {}}
    cur, kind = None, None
    for line in c3.splitlines():
        s = line.strip()
        m = re.match(r"ROW (\S+) \(E\d+\) N=(\d+) k=(\d+)", s)
        if m:
            cur, kind = m.group(1), "rows"
            census["rows"][cur] = {"N": int(m.group(2)), "k": int(m.group(3)),
                                   "log2_l": orders[cur]["log2_l"], "lanes": {}}
            continue
        m = re.match(r"PRIME_CONTROL (\S+) N=(\d+)", s)
        if m:
            cur, kind = m.group(1), "prime_controls"
            census["prime_controls"][cur] = {"N": int(m.group(2)), "log2_l": orders[cur]["log2_l"], "lanes": {}}
            continue
        m = re.match(r"FIXTURE (\S+) ", s)
        if m:
            cur, kind = m.group(1), "fixtures"
            census["fixtures"][cur] = {"lanes": {}}
            continue
        m = re.match(r"CELL c=(\d+) role=(\S+) n=(\d+) period=.*? m_span=(\d+) .* collapsed=(True|False)", s)
        if m and cur is not None:
            lane = {"c": int(m.group(1)), "n": int(m.group(3)), "m_span": int(m.group(4)),
                    "collapsed": m.group(5) == "True"}
            census[kind][cur]["lanes"][m.group(2)] = lane
        if s.startswith("MMT_TABLE3_DIFF"):
            cur = None
    return census, sc["C-4"]["output_run2"]


def run_cost_table(census_path, model_overrides=None):
    ct = load_block("cost_table")
    if model_overrides:
        ct.MODEL.update(model_overrides)
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        ct.main(["--census", census_path])
    return buf.getvalue()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    census, c4 = build()
    json.dump(census, open("rt_census_lite.json", "w"), indent=1, sort_keys=True)
    out = run_cost_table("rt_census_lite.json")
    open("rt_cost_table_rerun.txt", "w").write(out)
    a = [l.rstrip() for l in c4.splitlines()]
    b = [l.rstrip() for l in out.splitlines()]
    diff = [(i, x, y) for i, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(a, b)) if x != y]
    print("lines frozen", len(a), "rerun", len(b), "differing lines", len(diff))
    for i, x, y in diff[:10]:
        print("  line", i + 1)
        print("   frozen:", x[:160])
        print("   rerun :", y[:160])

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PTM-A, PTM-C (and variant PTM-C'), PTM-D against the plan's failure_signature.
Review computations only: coefficient arithmetic in F_(2^176) on a non-declared
fixture, synthetic census rows through the committed cost_table, and synthetic
cells through the committed decision_rules. No point, group order, cover,
relation or decision statistic on any declared cell; no driver run; no RUN-*."""
import contextlib
import copy
import io
import json
import math
import random
import re

from rt_census_lite import load_block, build

OUT = {}
ct = load_block("cost_table")
dr = load_block("decision_rules")
s0 = load_block("stage0_census")
census, c4_frozen = build()
c3 = __import__("yaml").safe_load(open(
    "/home/user/crypto-autoresearcher/coordination/goals/GOAL-ECDLP2M-001/batches/BATCH-2e63c3/design/"
    "TASK-20261002-9f9ce5/proof-search-map-audit.yaml", encoding="utf-8").read())["audit_sheet"]["session_computations"]["C-3"]["output_run2"]


def run_ct(cen, overrides=None):
    mod = load_block("cost_table")
    if overrides:
        mod.MODEL.update(overrides)
    path = "rt_ptm_census_tmp.json"
    json.dump(cen, open(path, "w"))
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        mod.main(["--census", path])
    return buf.getvalue()


def arm_cell_input(lane, cost_available=False):
    """ARM-CELL input exactly as the spec's procedure states it."""
    m = lane["m_span"]
    if m == 1:
        g_min = 1
    elif m < 13:
        g_min = 2 ** (m - 1)
    else:
        g_min = 2 ** (m - 1) - 1
    return {"n": lane["n"], "collapsed": lane["collapsed"],
            "l_coprime_def_field_order": lane.get("l_coprime_def_field_order"),
            "g_min": g_min, "cond7": lane.get("cond7", True), "regime_ratio": g_min / lane["c"],
            "cost_available": cost_available}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- PTM-A
ptma = {"lattice_from_C3": {}, "cost_branch_lines": [], "relabel_through_main_loop": {}, "cell_verdicts": {}}
for name in ("c2tnb191v1", "c2tnb239v1"):
    m = re.search(r"PRIME_CONTROL %s N=(\d+) N_prime=(\w+) divisor_lattice=(\[[^\]]*\])" % name, c3)
    ptma["lattice_from_C3"][name] = {"N": int(m.group(1)), "N_prime": m.group(2), "lattice": m.group(3)}
    pc = census["prime_controls"][name]
    # cell_verdict for every lane, ARM-CELL input rule (cond7 printed True on both lanes)
    for role, lane in pc["lanes"].items():
        lane = dict(lane, cond7=True)
        ptma["cell_verdicts"]["%s %s" % (name, role)] = dr.cell_verdict(arm_cell_input(lane))
    # adversarial relabelling: put the prime lane under every cost role so the main loop's FILTER is exercised
    k_stub = 1  # matched rho for prime rows has no Frobenius factor; k=1 gives sqrt(pi l / 4)
    row = {"N": pc["N"], "k": k_stub, "log2_l": pc["log2_l"],
           "lanes": {r: dict(pc["lanes"]["OPEN_N%d" % pc["N"]]) for r in ct.COST_ROLES}}
    cen = {"rows": {name: row}, "prime_controls": {}, "fixtures": {"KOBLITZ-176": census["fixtures"]["KOBLITZ-176"]}}
    out = run_ct(cen)
    ptma["relabel_through_main_loop"][name] = [l.strip() for l in out.splitlines() if l.strip().startswith("LANE")]
ptma["cost_branch_lines"] = [l.strip() for l in c4_frozen.splitlines() if "c2tnb" in l]
OUT["PTM-A"] = ptma

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- PTM-C (as specified)
kob = census["fixtures"]["KOBLITZ-176"]["lanes"]
ptmc = {"m_per_lane": {r: l["m_span"] for r, l in kob.items()},
        "cost_branch_lines": [l.strip() for l in c4_frozen.splitlines() if "KOBLITZ" in l]}
# through the main cost loop, lanes keyed by DECLARED role (OPEN_N<n> where c = jk)
declared = {}
for role, lane in kob.items():
    c = lane["c"]
    declared[s0.declared_role_deployed(c, 176)] = dict(lane)
row = {"N": 176, "k": 11, "log2_l": census["rows"]["c2pnb176v1"]["log2_l"], "lanes": declared}
out = run_ct({"rows": {"KOBLITZ-176(as row)": row}, "prime_controls": {}, "fixtures": {"KOBLITZ-176": census["fixtures"]["KOBLITZ-176"]}})
ptmc["main_loop_lines"] = [l.strip() for l in out.splitlines() if l.strip().startswith("LANE")]
ptmc["cell_verdicts"] = {r: dr.cell_verdict(arm_cell_input(dict(l, cond7=True))) for r, l in kob.items()}
ptmc["arm_cell_in_declared_grid"] = any(fx == "KOBLITZ-176" and arm == "ARM-CELL" for fx, arm, _ in dr.declared_grid())
OUT["PTM-C"] = ptmc

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- PTM-C' (K-isomorphic re-representation)
# y^2 + xy = x^3 + A' x^2 + 1 with A' = s^2 + s is K-isomorphic to y^2 + xy = x^3 + 1 (substitute y -> y + s x).
params = s0.parse_dump(open("rt_params.txt").read())
F = s0.GF2m(params["c2pnb176v1"]["poly"])
divs = s0.divisors(F.deg)
rng = random.Random(20261017)
s = rng.getrandbits(176)
A2 = F.sqr(s) ^ s
B2 = 1
dA2 = s0.smallest_subfield(F, A2, divs)
dB2 = s0.smallest_subfield(F, B2, divs)
d_ab2 = s0.lcm(dA2, dB2)
trA2 = F.trace_to_f2(A2)
cells2 = s0.census_cells(F, A2, B2, d_ab2, trA2, lambda _d: None, s0.declared_role_deployed, None)
lanes2 = {cell["role"]: cell for cell in cells2}
row2 = {"N": 176, "k": 11, "log2_l": census["rows"]["c2pnb176v1"]["log2_l"], "lanes": lanes2}
out2 = run_ct({"rows": {"KOBLITZ-176-reRep": row2}, "prime_controls": {}, "fixtures": {"KOBLITZ-176": census["fixtures"]["KOBLITZ-176"]}})
ptmc2 = {"s_seed": 20261017, "s": hex(s), "A_prime": hex(A2), "dA_prime": dA2, "dB": dB2, "d_AB": d_ab2,
         "TrA_prime": trA2,
         "isomorphism": "y -> y + s x maps y^2+xy=x^3+1 to y^2+xy=x^3+(s^2+s)x^2+1 over K = F_(2^176)",
         "lanes": {r: {"c": l["c"], "n": l["n"], "m_span": l["m_span"], "collapsed": l["collapsed"],
                       "cond7": l["cond7"]} for r, l in lanes2.items()},
         "cost_table_main_loop_lines": [l.strip() for l in out2.splitlines() if l.strip().startswith(("ROW", "LANE"))],
         "cell_verdicts": {r: dr.cell_verdict(arm_cell_input(l, cost_available=True)) for r, l in lanes2.items()}}
OUT["PTM-C-prime"] = ptmc2

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- PTM-D
P_GRID = [10, 20, 30, 31, 32, 34, 36, 37, 40]
ptmd = {"committed_code_lines_by_log2P": {}, "ic_path_composition": {}, "reference_rho_optimum": {}}
for lp in P_GRID:
    out = run_ct(census, {"P_REF": 2 ** lp})
    ptmd["committed_code_lines_by_log2P"][lp] = [l.strip() for l in out.splitlines() if "rho-as-IC" in l]


def ic_path_fc(work, mem, P, area):
    """The committed ic_arm FC composition for a single relation-collection-shaped phase:
    lse2(P, mem - area) + work - P (copied from cost_table.ic_arm, area_rel + work_rel - lp)."""
    return ct.lse2(math.log2(P), mem - math.log2(area)) + work - math.log2(P)


for name, row in census["rows"].items():
    Lb, k, N = row["log2_l"], row["k"], row["N"]
    res = {}
    for lp in P_GRID:
        P = 2 ** lp
        area = ct.MODEL["RHO_AREA_BITS_PER_PROC"]
        rho = ct.rho_arm(Lb, k, N, P, area)
        a_fc = ic_path_fc(rho["work"], rho["mem"], P, area)
        mem40 = 40 + math.log2(ct.MODEL["DP_BITS_FACTOR"] * Lb)
        b_fc = ic_path_fc(rho["work"], mem40, P, area)
        # reference: rho at its own FC-optimal DP table under MM-1 prices, x* = P sqrt(area / bits)
        bits = ct.MODEL["DP_BITS_FACTOR"] * Lb
        x_opt = math.log2(P) + 0.5 * math.log2(area / bits)
        W, t = rho["iters"], math.log2(ct.MODEL["RHO_MULTS_PER_ITER"]) + 2 * math.log2(N)
        rho_opt_fc = ct.lse2(math.log2(P), x_opt + math.log2(bits) - math.log2(area)) + ct.lse2(W - math.log2(P), W - x_opt) + t
        # reference: VOW's own cost-optimal ratio w/m = 3.8e8 / 2.5e7 (KN-LIT-73f7e1)
        x_vow = math.log2(P) + math.log2(3.8e8 / 2.5e7)
        rho_vow_fc = ct.lse2(math.log2(P), x_vow + math.log2(bits) - math.log2(area)) + ct.lse2(W - math.log2(P), W - x_vow) + t
        res[lp] = {"a_ic_path_d_fc": round(a_fc - rho["fc"], 4),
                   "b_ic_path_d_fc": round(b_fc - rho["fc"], 3),
                   "b_d_mem_vs_contract_rho": round(mem40 - rho["mem"], 3),
                   "contract_rho_fc_minus_optimum_rho_fc": round(rho["fc"] - rho_opt_fc, 3),
                   "b_d_fc_vs_rho_at_MM1_optimum": round(b_fc - rho_opt_fc, 3),
                   "b_d_fc_vs_rho_at_VOW_ratio": round(b_fc - rho_vow_fc, 3),
                   "log2_entries_rho_contract": round(math.log2(P) + 10, 2),
                   "log2_entries_rho_MM1_opt": round(x_opt, 2), "log2_entries_rho_VOW_ratio": round(x_vow, 2)}
    ptmd["ic_path_composition"][name] = res
OUT["PTM-D"] = ptmd
json.dump(OUT, open("rt_ptm_out.json", "w"), indent=1, default=str)

# ---- printed summary
print("PTM-A lattice:", ptma["lattice_from_C3"])
print("PTM-A verdicts:", ptma["cell_verdicts"])
print("PTM-A cost branch:", ptma["cost_branch_lines"])
print("PTM-A relabelled through main loop:", ptma["relabel_through_main_loop"])
print("PTM-C m per lane:", ptmc["m_per_lane"])
print("PTM-C main loop:", ptmc["main_loop_lines"])
print("PTM-C verdicts:", ptmc["cell_verdicts"], "ARM-CELL KOBLITZ in declared grid:", ptmc["arm_cell_in_declared_grid"])
print("PTM-C' A'=%s dA'=%d d_AB=%d TrA'=%d" % (ptmc2["A_prime"][:20] + "...", dA2, d_ab2, trA2))
for l in ptmc2["cost_table_main_loop_lines"]:
    print("PTM-C' ", l[:250])
print("PTM-C' verdicts:", ptmc2["cell_verdicts"])
for lp in P_GRID:
    print("PTM-D committed log2P=%d" % lp, ptmd["committed_code_lines_by_log2P"][lp][-1])
for lp in P_GRID:
    print("PTM-D c2pnb368w1 log2P=%d" % lp, ptmd["ic_path_composition"]["c2pnb368w1"][lp])

class Folded(str):
    pass


def to_folded(o):
    if isinstance(o, dict):
        return {k: to_folded(v) for k, v in o.items()}
    if isinstance(o, list):
        return [to_folded(v) for v in o]
    if isinstance(o, str) and (" " in o or ": " in o):
        return Folded(" ".join(o.split()))
    return o


def folded_rep(dumper, data):
    return dumper.represent_scalar("tag:yaml.org,2002:str", str(data), style=">")


yaml.SafeDumper.add_representer(Folded, folded_rep)

=== PAGE 1 ===
A double large prime variation for small genus hyperelliptic
index calculus
P. Gaudry, E. Thome, N. Theriault and C. Diem
November 21, 2005
Abstract
In this article, we examine how the index calculus approach for computing discrete loga-
rithms in small genus hyperelliptic curves can be improved by introducing a double large prime
variation. Two algorithms are presented. The rst algorithm is a rather natural adaptation
of the double large prime variation to the intended context. On heuristic and experimental
grounds, it seems to perform quite well but lacks a complete and precise analysis. Our second
algorithm is a considerably simplied variant, which can be analyzed easily. The resulting
complexity improves on the fastest known algorithms. Computer experiments show that for
hyperelliptic curves of genus three, our rst algorithm surpasses Pollard’s Rho method even
for rather small eld sizes.
1 Introduction
The discrete logarithm problem in the jacobian group of a curve is known to be solvable in
subexponential time if the genus is large compared to the base eld size [1, 20, 8, 9, 14, 6]. The
corresponding index calculus algorithm also works for small xed genus, and although the running
time becomes exponential it can still be better than Pollard’s Rho algorithm [11]. Introducing a
large prime variation [23], it is possible to obtain an index calculus algorithm that is asymptotically
faster than Pollard’s Rho algorithm already for genus 3 curves.
In the present work, we go one step further in this direction and introduce a double large prime
variation for the small genus index calculus. Our algorithm is a simple extension to the single large
prime algorithm of [23]. However, making a rigorous analysis is not that easy: Double large prime
variations are commonly used in factorization algorithms and analyzed empirically. In order to
obtain a proven complexity result, we introduce a simplied algorithm for the double large prime
variation which lends itself much better to a rigorous complexity analysis. The analysis is made
for xed genus and growing eld size. Our proof is valid for the restricted context of hyperelliptic
curves in imaginary Weierstrass form with cyclic jacobian group, and the complexity result is
stated as follows.
Theorem 1. Let g  3 be xed. Let C be a hyperelliptic curve of genus g over Fq given by an
imaginary Weierstrass equation, such that the jacobian group JacC(Fq) is cyclic. Then the discrete
logarithm problem in JacC(Fq) can be solved in expected time
eO

q2 2
g

as q tends to innity.
The eO-notation captures logarithmic factors. This complexity improves on the previous best
bound eO(q2 2
g+1=2 ). The presented algorithm also applies to general curves of genus g  3, not
2000 Mathematics Subject Classication. Primary 11Y16; Secondary 11T71, 94A60.
1
=== PAGE 2 ===
necessarily hyperelliptic and not necessarily with cyclic jacobian group (but provided that the
Jacobian arithmetic can be performed in polynomial time). Heuristically, the complexity result
still holds.
The improvement is negligible for curves of large genus and therefore the case of genus 3
curves is given special consideration. For genus 3 curves, Pollard’s Rho method has a running
time in eO(q1:5), whereas the single large prime algorithm is in eO(q1:428:::) and our new method
is in eO(q1:333:::). We did practical experiments that demonstrate that even when the jacobian
group has relatively small size, our algorithm is much faster than Pollard’s Rho algorithm. In
these comparisons, we consider only curves whose jacobian group is of almost prime order, so
that splitting the discrete problem in smaller problems in subgroups [22] is not possible. This
is the case for instances that occur in the context of cryptography. Therefore, when designing a
cryptosystem [16] based on a genus 3 curve, it is necessary to take into account our attack, and not
only Pollard’s Rho attack. The sizes of the parameters should then be enlarged by about 12.5%
to maintain the security level.
The article is organized as follows: In Section 2, we x the general setting and recall previous
work. Our double large prime variation is introduced in Section 3, together with our simplied
variant. This simplied variant is analyzed in Section 4. In Section 5, we describe our computer
experiments that validate our approach and show that it outperforms Pollard’s Rho method rather
early. Section 6 explores the relationship between our \full" and \simplied" algorithms, as well
as the relevance of our algorithm beyond the restricted context of hyperelliptic curves with cyclic
jacobian group.
The order of the authors is chronological. The rst two authors found the algorithm and gave
a heuristic analysis. A complete proof was obtained by the rst three authors. The fourth author
then gave a much simpler proof, and the proof of Theorem 1 presented in this work follows the
ideas of the fourth author.
Acknowledgements
The rst three authors thank Antoine Lejay who helped with the probabilistic statements that
occurred in the rst proof of Theorem 1.
2 Setting and previous work
2.1 Setting
Let C be a hyperelliptic curve of genus g  3 over a nite eld Fq with q elements, given by an
imaginary Weierstrass equation. The elements of the jacobian group JacC(Fq) of C over Fq are
handled via their Mumford representation [19]: a divisor class contains a unique reduced divisor
that is represented by a pair of polynomials hu(x); v(x)i. The degree of u(x) is called the weight
of the reduced divisor and a reduced divisor is called prime if u(x) is irreducible.
A discrete logarithm problem in JacC(Fq) is to be solved. Namely, we work in a cyclic subgroup
G of JacC(Fq). A generating reduced divisor D1 of G and another reduced divisor D2 2 G are
given. The goal is to compute the integer  in [0; #G  1] such that D2 = D1 in JacC(Fq). The
group order is also supposed to be part of the input; in our case, since the genus is xed, it can
be computed in polynomial time [21].
The algorithms we are dealing with have a complexity which is exponential in log q. Since
any task that takes a time which is polynomial in log q is considered easy, we shall often use the
eO()-notation for complexity estimates: A function in eO(f(q)) is a function that is bounded by
f(q) times a polynomial in log q for large enough q.
2
=== PAGE 3 ===
2.2 Basic index calculus
The general index calculus algorithm proceeds as follows: A factor base B that consists of prime
divisors of low weight is formed. Then random linear combinations of D1 and D2 are computed
using, for instance, Cantor’s algorithm [3]. For each combination, one checks whether it can be
written as a sum of elements of the factor base by factoring the u-polynomial of its Mumford
representation. If this is the case, then we have a useful relation and the corresponding data is put
in a row of a matrix. After enough relations have been found, there exists a non trivial combination
of the rows that sums to zero; this is a simple linear algebra problem. Since each row represents
a linear combination of D1 and D2, any combination of rows also represents a linear combination
of D1 and D2 that can be computed. We can then nd  and  such that D1 + D2 = 0. This
gives the solution to the discrete logarithm problem as long as  is invertible modulo #G, which
will be the case with large probability.
For (small) xed genus, the prime divisors considered for the factor base are divisors of weight 1.
This \basic index calculus"algorithm has therefore complexity eO(q2), split in eO(q) for the relation
search and eO(q2) for the linear algebra.
An optimized variant of the basic index calculus algorithm, due to Harley, consists in balancing
the relation search and linear algebra steps by restricting the factor base size to qr elements, with
0 < r < 1. With the best value of r = 1  1=(g + 1), the complexity becomes eO(q2 2
g+1 ).
We shall not give more details on the basic technique of index calculus and refer the reader
to [23] for a complete description.
2.3 Single large prime variation
Extending the idea of the \balanced" index calculus approach, a single large prime variation has

6.2 Full algorithm and random graphs
We used experiments in order to get an idea of the behaviour of the cycle lengths in the full
algorithm, but, as we said before, it is hard to guess an asymptotic behaviour from these. Another
approach to make conjectures is to consider the LP-graph as a random graph perturbed by the
special vertex 1 and the numerous edges attached to it due to FP relations. At the end of the
computation we expect as many as O(b q2 2

important for high genera.
We mention two theoretical results from the literature on random graphs. The rst suggests
the cycle length might be exponential, but is probably too pessimistic. The second suggests
polynomial cycle length, but is probably too optimistic.
In [10], it is proven that the rst cycle in a random graph appears once #L=2 edges are included
and the length of the rst cycle is of order ((#L)1=6). It is also proven that for any constant k,
the k-th cycle has a length of order ((#L)1=6 log(#L)k1). These lengths would be too large in
our context. This result does not capture our situation for two reasons: First, we need to estimate
the length of a large quantity of cycles, and the analysis of [10] is valid only for the rst few cycles.
In particular, it assumes that the cycles are in disjoint components, which is not the case in the
end of the relation search. Second, the presence of the FP relations is enough to make the rst
cycle appear earlier than would be expected otherwise.
The other theoretical result is taken from [4]: the diameter of a random graph is O(log(#L))
if the number of edges is a constant bigger than 1=2  #L. This estimate for the diameter would
be perfect for our analysis. However in the full algorithm the relations are built on the y as soon
as cycles appear, so that we cannot deduce a useful bound for the cycle lengths, except maybe at
the very end of the relation search. It is also not clear that the algorithm stops at a point where
the graph is dense enough to have the appropriate diameter.
6.3 Memory requirement
For the simplied algorithm, the memory requirement during the linear algebra step is in eO(q1 1
g ).
In the full algorithm this might be larger if the cycle length cannot be bounded by a polynomial
in log q.
For the relation collection, the estimate of the memory requirement is in eO(q), if a nave
implementation is used for the LP-graph. Indeed, there are #L = O(q) vertices in the graph and
since no edge that would create a cycle is ever stored in the LP-graph, there are at most O(q)
edges, so we need O(q) memory to store the LP-graph information.
In the case of the full algorithm we cannot hope for a better storage requirement, since the
experiments suggests that (q) edges are indeed needed before having enough relations.
On the other hand, in the simplied algorithm, at the end of Phase 2, the LP-graph has

used. Choosing an appropriate data structure the memory requirement drops to eO(Nmax) (with
a possible loss of a log q factor in the time complexity, in order to handle the data structure).
Hence the memory requirement of the simplied algorithm can be made smaller than for the
full algorithm by an exponential factor. This should be kept in mind for practical applications,
when the memory might be problematic. A reasonable approach might be to implement a mixture
between the full and the simplied algorithm, where we keep the memory low but still make use
of the FP relations.

6.4 Relevance to more general context
We now provide heuristic arguments backing the validity of our approach to a broader context.
We have restricted our proof to the case of hyperelliptic curves of cyclic jacobian group given
by an imaginary Weierstrass equation. If the jacobian group is not cyclic, our analysis is not
valid. However, as soon as the group structure is known, we can follow the randomizing strategy
of Section 7 in [9] to produce uniformly random elements in the whole group.
Furthermore, the results are formulated only for the context of hyperelliptic curves, but on
heuristic basis our algorithm should perform equally well for general curves.
General setting
For any xed genus g, we consider a family of curves over a nite eld Fq with q elements, where
q grows to innity. We assume that the curves are given in the following representation, which
is more suitable from the algorithmic point of view. Let C be a curve in the family. Even if
the practical models are ane or singular, we actually consider a complete non-singular curve
associated to it, and the notation C is reserved for this non-singular model. The algorithmic
assumptions are the following:
 There exists a rational point P1 2 C(Fq). This is true for any curve as long as q is large
enough.
 The group structure of JacC(Fq) is known. Namely we have an explicit set of generators G1,
. . . , Gk, of known orders such that JacC(Fq) = hG1i      hGki.
 We have a probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in log q to perform the group
operations in JacC(Fq). The elements are represented by divisors in the form E  wP1,
where E is an eective divisor of degree w  g and w is minimal. Such an E exists and is
unique in each class, and E  wP1 is called a reduced divisor.
 We have a probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in log q to decompose an
eective divisor as the sum of its prime divisors.
Apart from the known group structure, these assumptions are veried in the classical case of
hyperelliptic curves given by an imaginary Weierstrass equation (using Mumford representation),
and for Cab curves. Also, if a curve is given by a plane equation of bounded degree, there are
algorithms available to perform the group operations in polynomial time [26, 15, 13].
In this setting, it is possible to dene the factor base and the large primes by partitioning the
set of eective divisor of degree 1 into sets of appropriate cardinalities. The descriptions of the
full and simplied algorithms for hyperelliptic curves extend easily, with Cantor’s algorithm and
Mumford representation replaced with their generalized equivalent notions. However, the proof of
the simplied algorithm does not follow, since it heavily relies on the statistical properties of large
primes given in Proposition 4. In the case of hyperelliptic curves, it was simple to estimate this
statistics, based on the properties of the Mumford representation with respect to the hyperelliptic
involution. Heuristically, there seems to be no reason why the statistics would behave dierently
for general curves, however a proof in the most general setting is out of the scope of this work,
and we keep to a heuristic result for non-hyperelliptic curves.
7 Conclusion
We have described two algorithms for solving discrete logarithms in curves of small genus at least 3.
The rst one is a traditional double large prime variant of the algorithm of [23] and its complexity
is heuristic. The second algorithm is a simplied variant that can be rigorously analyzed in the
context of cyclic jacobian groups of hyperelliptic curves. The complexity is better than previously
known methods and experiments demonstrated that even for rather small sizes, our method is
14
=== PAGE 15 ===
faster than Pollard Rho algorithm. On the other hand, the space requirement is much larger and
can become problematic.
The direct application to cryptography is that the security of a genus 3 cryptosystem is over-
estimated if only Pollard’s Rho algorithm is taken into account. Indeed, we have shown that the
running time for solving a discrete logarithm problem in a genus 3 jacobian group has a complex-
ity similar to a discrete logarithm computation in an elliptic curve for which the logarithm of the
group order is 1/9th smaller. We therefore recommend to enlarge the group-size by 12.5%.
The complexity of our attack, as for any index calculus method, depends only on the size of
the whole jacobian group. Hence we are in a situation somewhat similar to multiplicative groups
of nite elds: It is possible to work in a subgroup and with a private key whose sizes are large
enough to counter Pollard Rho and similar attacks, as long as the size of the whole group is large
enough to prevent an index calculus attack.
We note that our method also applies to the Weil descent algorithm of [12] that attacks elliptic
curves dened over small extension elds. Hence, this asymptotic 12.5% penalty also applies to
elliptic curve cryptosystems dened over extension nite elds whose degree is a multiple of 3.
Finally, we would like to point out that an alternative double large prime method that uses
smooth functions instead of divisors has recently been proposed [7] for the non-hyperelliptic setting.
A heuristic complexity analysis indicates that this algorithm can solve the discrete logarithm
problem in jacobian groups of non-hyperelliptic curves of genus 3 over Fq in time of eO(q).
